whatItDoes: Performs IPv6 address calculations in the browser. Expand, compress, sort, and summarize IPv6 addresses, compute the network prefix, and enumerate the range of hosts covered by a CIDR block. Applies the RFC 4291 rules for leading-zero removal, case mapping, and the double-colon compression.
whyItExists: IPv6 addresses are long and easy to mistype, and IPv6 subnets follow different rules than IPv4. Network engineers need a reliable tool to expand compressed addresses, derive the network and interface IDs, and understand how many addresses a prefix covers.
whoShouldUse: Network engineers planning IPv6 deployments, DevOps engineers writing firewall and routing configs, security analysts auditing address ranges, and students learning IPv6 addressing.
useCases: Expand a compressed IPv6 address like 2001:db8::1 to its full form
Compress a long hexadecimal address to its shortest representation
Find the network prefix and host range for a CIDR block like /48
Confirm whether an address is link-local, unique-local, or global
instructions: Paste an IPv6 address in the input field
View the expanded and compressed forms side by side
Optionally add a /prefix to compute the network and available hosts
Read the scope classification (global, unique-local, link-local)
Copy any result you need for your configuration
bestPractices: Always validate the neighbor ID with NDP rather than assuming reachability
Use the compressed form for configuration but the expanded form when comparing bit-by-bit
Treat /64 as the standard subnet size for most networks
Remember that IPv6 subnets are dramatically larger than IPv4 for several orders of magnitude
commonMistakes: Writing a single-digit group as 0x rather than 0000 when expanding
Applying IPv4-style subnet-host math to an IPv6 prefix
Confusing the double-colon with an ellipsis and dropping parts
Assuming link-local addresses are globally routable
faq: What is the double colon in IPv6? — It represents the longest run of trailing zero hextets and can appear only once in an address.
How many addresses are in a /48? — 2^(128-48) = 2^80 addresses.
Does this tool validate addresses? — Yes, it rejects malformed addresses and unwanted cases with a clear error.
Is calculation local? — All processing happens in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
